newsitem.title: USA: Oil prices rise on supply worries, grains rally.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices rise on supply worries, grains rally.

text.p: Oil prices posted strong gains on declines in U.S. crude and gasoline stocks, and grain prices rose as traders guessed that Hurricane Fran would not bring needed rains as far inland as the Corn Belt.
Fran, expected to batter the Carolina coastline by Friday with damaging winds and rain, also prompted buying in lumber futures on ideas of more lumber demand.
But cotton prices continued to ease as fears of damage to Southeast crop areas faded.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange October delivery crude oil closed 20 cents a barrel higher at $23.44, and October unleaded gasoline closed up 1.45 cents per gallon at 64.41. October heating oil closed up 0.82 cent per gallon at 65.03.

Traders said nervousness about Iraq and Mideast oil supplies continued to discourage sellers. But the immediate reason for buying was weekly data from the American Petroleum Institute confirming tight domestic stockpiles.
The API reported after the close of trading on Wednesday that U.S. crude oil stocks fell 5.68 million barrels in the week ended Aug. 30 to 313.15 million barrels.
Gasoline stocks fell 3.71 million barrels to 192.82 million from 196.53 million barrels. Distillate or heating oil stocks rose 3.24 million barrels to 108.90 million.

The API data came on the heels of Iraq's latest confrontation with the United States, which in turn forced an indefinite delay in the implementation of a U.N. deal reached in May to allow Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil to pay for food and medical supplies.
That oil, about 700,000 barrels a day, had been expected to start arriving in world markets this month.
"(The Iraqi oil sale delay) will certainly have a physical impact and on top of that there is this speculative factor," said Cyrus Tahmassebi of Energy Trends Inc. in Washington.
"There is a fear in the market that things could get out of control," he said.
That was also the fear with Hurricane Fran, which was packing winds of 115 miles per hour (185 kmh) as it moved toward the Carolinas on Thursday afternoon.
The storm had already dumped more than 12 inches of rain on the mid-Atlantic seaboard in the previous 24 hours.

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, November lumber futures ended $8.60 higher at $396 per thousand board feet as traders expected Fran's aftermath to include a strong boost in lumber demand to repair storm damage.

Low retail lumber inventories have already forced dealers to pay the higher prices quoted by saw mills in recent months. Strong demand by home builders has kept lumber flowing through marketing channels despite the higher prices, analysts said.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, Fran also played a role in higher prices as weather forecasts at midday predicted that the storm's moisture would likely miss the dry eastern Corn Belt and provide no late boost for corn and soybean growth.
December corn closed 1-1/4 cents per bushel higher at $3.34-3/4, and November soybeans ended 15-1/2 cents per bushel higher at $7.95-3/4.

The National Weather Service six-to-10 day forecast late on Wednesday also predicted below-normal temperatures and normal to below normal rainfall for nearly all key U.S. soybean growing regions for next week.
"The six-to-10 day was cool and dry and what it needs is warm and wet," said Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter Reynolds. "We need rain and we're not getting it."
At the New York Cotton Exchange prices closed lower as fears of possible storm damage faded. December cotton closed down 1.98 cents at 73.64 cents a pound.
"There is just isn't anything out there to support the market," said Judy Ganes of Merrill Lynch, adding that prices face further pressure as the Southern harvest gets under way.
